events.title: Apple introduces the iPod
events.description: A pocket-sized digital music player becomes a new product for the computer maker.

events.title: Microsoft and the US government propose a settlement
events.description: The agreement would restrict some business practices. Court review and other legal steps remain.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina strikes
events.description: The hurricane devastates Gulf Coast communities and creates an enormous need for rescue and recovery.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple grew to about $9.93 per starting dollar, Boeing to $2.57 and Microsoft to $1.23. The international share basket also more than doubled. The starting point came after the September attacks, so losses before September 2001 were already reflected in prices. A later gain does not make a frightening event an automatic buying signal.

Boeing launched its 7E7 aircraft project in 2004 with an order from ANA for 50 planes; it reported 126 customer commitments by year-end. Apple introduced iPod and said two million had sold by early 2004. Microsoft announced a $3-per-share special dividend in 2004. These are three different business stories, and none promises a particular share return.

Later in the window, euro notes and coins entered everyday use. The Columbia shuttle was lost in 2003, and Katrina struck the Gulf Coast in 2005. These events changed people’s lives while businesses responded to many pressures. Boeing’s stock gain contrasts with planned job cuts at the start: bad news does not give a precise forecast, just as a product launch does not promise a gain.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: People were mourning, helping one another and reviewing safety. Airlines and aircraft makers were adjusting plans amid uncertainty.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: The period after the investment began determined the result. Different companies recovered differently, and the broad baskets did not depend on one product or industry.
reflection.what_faded_away: An announced job cut did not reveal a company’s five-year stock return. A coming software launch did not either.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: Nobody had a map of the recovery or the future leaders. Seeing Apple’s eventual gain now can hide how uncertain its prospects were then.

hot:2001-09:boeing.text: Boeing began the 7E7 program in April 2004 after ANA ordered 50 planes. In January 2005, it reported 126 orders and commitments announced during 2004. These plans gave it a large new aircraft project, but it still had to build and deliver the planes to turn orders into sales.

hot:2001-09:microsoft.text: Microsoft announced a one-time $3-per-share dividend in July 2004, payable in December, along with regular dividends and a large share-buyback plan. The special payment returned cash to shareholders in addition to the company’s regular dividend.

hot:2001-09:apple.text: Apple introduced the iPod in October 2001, and by January 2004 said more than two million had sold. The portable music player gave Apple a product business beside Mac computers and helped make its iTunes software more useful to customers.
